items.p: Which questions does an economic system answer?
items.a: What to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce
w: When to pay taxes and how much
items.ref: An economic system answers: what to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce.

items.p: What is the main difference between economic systems?
items.a: How much influence the government has on production and distribution
w: The language spoken in the country
items.ref: The differences concern the amount of influence that the government has on the production and distribution of goods and services.

items.p: In a free-market economy, what is the economy based on?
items.a: The market forces of supply and demand
w: A plan written every five years
items.ref: The economy is based on the market forces of supply and demand, and the government has little or no control.

items.p: In a command (planned) economy, who establishes the prices?
items.a: The government
items.ref: The government is in complete control of the economy and prices are established by the government.

items.p: Which is the most common economic system in the modern world?
items.a: The mixed economy
items.ref: The mixed economy is the most common economic system in the modern world, typical of European countries.

items.p: What is the public sector?
items.a: The part of the economy controlled by the state
w: The part of the economy run only by private companies
items.ref: It is the part of the economy that is controlled by the state, formed by public corporations.

items.p: How are public corporations paid for?
items.a: With money raised from taxation
items.ref: These corporations provide goods and services for the citizens and are paid for with money raised from taxation.

items.p: Why did many governments privatise public corporations at the end of the 20th century?
items.a: To make them more efficient and profitable
w: To give them to other countries
items.ref: Many governments started to privatise some public corporations in order to make them more efficient and profitable.

items.p: What is remunicipalisation?
items.a: A revival of public ownership at a local level
w: The sale of all public services to private companies
The building of new town halls
items.ref: In the last two decades we witnessed a revival of public ownership at a local level, known as remunicipalisation.

items.p: Which is a disadvantage of the public sector?
items.a: Increased bureaucracy and slow decision-making
w: Lower and stable prices for essential industries
Profits go back to the government
items.ref: Disadvantages: increased bureaucracy and slow decision-making, political influence, lack of competition, losses paid through taxes.

items.p: What is the GDP (Gross Domestic Product)?
items.a: The total value of goods and services produced within the borders of a nation in a year
w: The total debt of a country
The number of people who work in a country
The money a country spends abroad
items.ref: GDP: total value of goods and services produced within the borders of a nation in a year.

items.p: What does GDP per capita indicate?
items.a: The average income of the citizens of a country
items.ref: GDP per capita is a country's GDP divided by its population: it indicates the average income of its citizens.

items.p: Which are the 4 phases of the business cycle?
items.a: Expansion, recession, depression, recovery
items.ref: The business cycle has 4 phases: expansion, recession, depression and recovery.

items.p: What happens to the purchasing power of money when prices rise?
items.a: It decreases
items.ref: When price level rises, the purchasing power of money decreases.

items.p: What is shrinkflation?
items.a: Reducing the size or quantity of a product while the price stays the same or rises
w: A fall in the number of workers
Making products bigger at the same price
items.ref: Shrinkflation is reducing or shrinking the size, quantity or weight of a product while the price remains the same or even increases.

items.p: What is natural capital?
items.a: Nature's contribution to the economy, such as water, air and land
w: The money of a national bank
The capital city of a country
The number of factories in a region
items.ref: Natural capital can be defined as nature's contribution to the economy: elements necessary for our survival (water, air, land).

items.p: What is the aim of the green economy?
items.a: Improving human well-being in the long run without exposing future generations to environmental risks
w: Producing as much as possible, whatever the cost
Reducing the number of products on the market
Increasing the price of all goods
items.ref: Green economy: activities resulting in an improvement of human well-being in the long run, without exposing future generations to environmental risks.

items.p: What is the problem with traditional measures of economic performance?
items.a: They do not consider natural capital
w: They are too expensive to calculate
They are used only in Europe
items.ref: Traditional measures of economic performance do not consider natural capital, and this is becoming unsustainable.

items.p: What is the solution suggested in the handout?
items.a: Integrating natural capital and green economy into economic decision making
items.ref: The solution is the integration of natural capital and green economy into economic decision making.

items.p: What do consumers look for today?
items.a: Environmentally friendly, socially responsible and sustainable products
items.ref: Today consumers look for environmentally friendly, socially responsible and sustainable products and services.

items.p: What does NEET mean?
items.a: Neither in Employment nor in Education or Training
items.ref: The NEET rate measures young people who are Neither in Employment nor in Education or Training.

items.p: Which age group does the NEET rate measure?
items.a: Young people aged 15-24
items.ref: It measures the percentage of young people aged 15-24.

items.p: What percentage of young people were NEET in 2020?
items.ref: In 2020, 22.4% of young people were NEET.

items.p: Who are the majority of NEET?
items.a: Girls and young women
items.ref: The majority of NEET are girls and young women, and the status tends to be more permanent for girls.

items.p: What is the main reason for the gender gap in NEET rates?
items.a: Family responsibilities
items.ref: The main reason is family responsibilities, which penalize girls especially in low and middle-income countries.
